title: Branch Prediction
summary: How a pipelined CPU guesses which way a branch goes so it doesn't have to stop and wait to find out.

blocks.markdown:
**Branch prediction** is a pipelined CPU guessing which way an `if` will go, instead of stopping to wait for the answer.

- A wrong guess undoes work — a **misprediction**.
- A right guess keeps the pipeline full, which is most of the time.
- The technique that makes deep pipelines actually fast in practice.
- See [pipeline-hazards](pipeline-hazards) for the problem this solves.

blocks.subTitle: Key terms
blocks.markdown:
The vocabulary for this topic.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Control hazard | Pipeline doesn't yet know the next instruction |
| Speculation | Guessing and running ahead before knowing the answer |
| BTB | Cache that remembers where a branch jumped to last time |

Everything below builds on these three.

A pipelined CPU fetches the next instruction before the current one finishes, to keep every stage busy.

- A **branch** (`if`, loop check, function return) decides *which* instruction comes next — taken or not-taken.
- That decision isn't known until the branch is **evaluated**, several stages later.
- Meanwhile the fetch stage doesn't know what to fetch. This stall is a **control hazard**.

blocks.subTitle: The naive fix is too slow
blocks.markdown:
The simplest fix: freeze fetch until the branch resolves, then fetch the right instruction.

- Correct, but every branch **stalls** the pipeline for several cycles.
- Branches are common — roughly one in every five to seven instructions.
- Stalling that often would erase most of the speedup pipelining was built for.

Instead of waiting, the CPU **predicts** the outcome and **speculates**: it fetches and executes down the guessed path before the branch is confirmed.

- If the guess is right, no time was lost — the work was already done.
- If wrong, that speculative work is thrown away and the pipeline restarts on the correct path.
- Predicting well, not avoiding the guess, is the real solution.

**Static prediction** picks a guess with a fixed rule, decided before the program runs — no history checked.

- **Always not-taken** — assume the branch falls through.
- **Always taken** — assume it jumps.
- **Backward taken, forward not-taken (BTFNT)** — loop branches jump backward and are usually taken; forward branches (error checks) usually aren't.

Simple and cheap, but blind to how a specific branch actually behaves.

**Dynamic prediction** watches each branch's actual **history** while the program runs and predicts from that.

- Each branch gets tracked separately using its instruction address.
- If a branch was taken the last few times, predict taken next time.
- Adapts to real behavior, so it beats static prediction on most code — at the cost of extra hardware to remember history.

Two strategies, two trade-offs.

| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Decides from | Fixed rule | Runtime history |
| Hardware cost | None | Counters, tables |

Dynamic adapts per-branch and wins on real workloads, which is why every modern CPU uses it.

The simplest dynamic predictor: one bit per branch, storing just the last outcome.

- Bit = 1 means predict **taken**; 0 means predict **not-taken**. After the branch resolves, the bit is set to what actually happened.
- Weak spot: a loop that runs 99 times then exits mispredicts **twice** — once on entry, once on exit — because one wrong outcome flips the whole guess.

A **2-bit saturating counter** fixes the 1-bit flaw by needing **two** wrong outcomes in a row to flip the prediction.

- Four states: strongly not-taken, weakly not-taken, weakly taken, strongly taken.
- Taken moves the counter up (capped at strongly taken); not-taken moves it down. "Saturating" means it stops at the ends instead of wrapping.
- One odd outcome no longer flips the guess — much better on loops.

Predicting taken/not-taken isn't enough — if taken, the CPU also needs to know **where** to jump to, before it decodes the branch.

- The **branch target buffer (BTB)** is a small cache: branch address in, its last jump target out.
- On a **BTB hit**, fetch starts at the predicted target immediately, no waiting for decode.
- Predictor says *taken or not*; BTB says *taken to where*. Both run together.

When a guess turns out wrong, everything fetched down the guessed path is invalid.

- The pipeline **flushes**: those in-flight instructions are discarded before they can change any state.
- Fetch restarts from the correct path — a **misprediction penalty** of several lost cycles.
- The deeper the pipeline, the more instructions were speculatively in flight, so the more cycles a flush wastes.

Modern CPUs go further than fetching ahead — they **execute** down the guessed path too, keeping results provisional.

- Provisional results wait in buffers, not the visible register file, until the branch is confirmed.
- Correct guess: results are **committed** as if nothing was speculative.
- Wrong guess: the CPU **rolls back**, discarding provisional results — this is what a misprediction flush is actually undoing.

blocks.sectionTitle: Why accuracy matters more as pipelines deepen
blocks.markdown:
A deeper pipeline (more stages) means more speculative instructions are in flight when a branch is finally resolved.

- A misprediction now flushes more work, so the **penalty grows** with pipeline depth.
- Going from 95% to 99% predictor accuracy matters far more on a 20-stage pipeline than a 5-stage one.
- This is why modern CPUs spend real chip area on prediction hardware instead of a simple 2-bit counter alone.

Common mistakes:

- **"Prediction avoids the hazard."** No — it only hides the cost when the guess is right; the control hazard is still there.
- **"Wrong guesses corrupt results."** No — speculative results stay provisional and are rolled back; architectural state is never wrong.
- **"A 2-bit counter is state of the art."** It's the teaching baseline; real CPUs combine it with global history and BTBs. See [hardware-security-side-channels](hardware-security-side-channels) for what speculation can leak.

blocks.subTitle: Why prediction is needed
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why do pipelined CPUs need branch prediction at all?**

A pipeline fetches ahead, but a branch's outcome isn't known until it's evaluated several stages later — a control hazard. Stalling until then would waste cycles on nearly every fifth instruction. Prediction lets fetch guess and keep going, so the pipeline stays full when the guess is right.

blocks.subTitle: Static vs dynamic
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Static vs dynamic branch prediction — what's the difference?**

Static uses a fixed rule decided before the program runs, like always-not-taken or backward-taken-forward-not-taken. Dynamic tracks each branch's actual history at runtime and predicts from that. Dynamic costs more hardware but adapts per branch, so it's what real CPUs use.

blocks.subTitle: 2-bit predictor
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does a 2-bit saturating counter improve on 1 bit?**

A 1-bit predictor flips its guess after a single wrong outcome, so a loop's exit mispredicts and then mispredicts again on re-entry. A 2-bit counter needs two wrong outcomes in a row to flip, since it has four states (strongly/weakly taken or not-taken). One-off exceptions no longer break the prediction for the whole loop.

blocks.subTitle: Misprediction penalty
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the misprediction penalty, and what drives its size?**

It's the number of cycles lost when a predicted branch turns out wrong: the pipeline flushes all speculative instructions fetched down the guessed path and restarts on the correct one. Pipeline depth drives its size — deeper pipelines have more speculative work in flight at any moment, so a flush throws away more.

blocks.subTitle: Branch target buffer
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a BTB and why is it needed alongside a predictor?**

The branch target buffer is a small cache mapping a branch's address to the target it jumped to last time. The predictor only says taken or not-taken; if taken, the CPU still needs an address to fetch from before the branch is even decoded. The BTB supplies that address so fetch doesn't stall waiting for decode.
